payment_diversion.title: Possible payment diversion
payment_diversion.summary: Money was paid to an account that may belong to a criminal, after banking details were changed. Speed matters: act on the first step now.

steps.title: Call your bank's fraud line now.
steps.why: Your bank is the only one who can try to stop or recall the payment. Minutes count.
do: Pick your bank below and call the official fraud line.
Say: "I made a payment to a fraudulent account. Please try to stop or recall it."
Have ready: the date, the amount and the account it went to.
Write down the reference number they give you.

steps.title: Confirm with your supplier on a number you already had.
steps.why: Do not reply to the email or call any number in it. The criminal may be reading that mailbox.
do: Phone the supplier on a number from an old invoice, your contacts or their website.
Ask: "Did you change your banking details?"
Tell them their email may also be hacked.

steps.title: Check your mailbox for hidden rules and strange sign-ins.
steps.why: Criminals often add a hidden rule that forwards or hides emails, so they can see payments coming.
do: Use a different, clean device if you can.
Look for forwarding and inbox rules you did not create, and delete them.
Check recent sign-ins for places or devices you don't recognise.
Change your email password and turn on two-step verification.

steps.title: Keep the evidence.
steps.why: The bank, SAPS and your insurer will ask for it. Don't delete the email.
do: Save the email with the "new banking details" (screenshot or download it).
Save the proof of payment.
Add them below. Mgadi fingerprints each file on this phone. Nothing is uploaded.

mailbox_compromise.title: Possible hacked mailbox
mailbox_compromise.summary: Someone may have access to your email. No payment has been mentioned, so the aim is to lock them out before they use it.

steps.title: Lock the account.
steps.why: Stop the criminal from reading or sending email as you.
do: From a clean device, change your email password.
Turn on two-step verification.
Sign out of all other sessions if your email offers it.

steps.title: Check for hidden rules and strange sign-ins.
steps.why: A hidden forwarding rule can keep leaking your email after you change the password.
do: Delete forwarding and inbox rules you did not create.
Check recent sign-ins for places or devices you don't recognise.

steps.title: Warn your clients and suppliers.
steps.why: Criminals use a hacked mailbox to send fake invoices to your contacts.
do: Phone or message your main clients: "Our email was hacked. We have NOT changed our banking details."
If money has left your account, call your bank's fraud line now.

steps.title: Keep the evidence.
steps.why: Screenshots of the rules and sign-ins help IT support and SAPS.
do: Screenshot the strange rules and sign-ins before you delete them, and add them below.

suspicious_message.title: Suspicious message, no money moved
suspicious_message.summary: Good news: it sounds like no money has left yet. Don't pay and don't click until you've checked.

steps.title: Don't pay, don't click, don't reply.
steps.why: A request to change banking details is the start of most payment-diversion scams.
do: Do not update any banking details from the message.
If you typed a password into a link, change it now from a clean device.
If you shared a PIN or OTP, call your bank's fraud line now.

steps.title: Check with the sender on a number you already had.
steps.why: The only safe check is a call to a number you trusted before this message arrived.
do: Phone the supplier or person on a number from an old invoice, your contacts or their website.

steps.title: Keep the message.
steps.why: It helps your bank warn others.
do: Screenshot or save the message and add it below. Then report it to your bank.

not_cyber.title: This may not be a cyber incident
not_cyber.summary: From what you described, this sounds like a normal payment or admin problem. Stay careful anyway.

steps.title: Double-check before you relax.
steps.why: Late payments and pending payments are common, but scams also start this way.
do: If anyone asked you to change banking details, treat it as suspicious and start again.
If money has left your account to an account you don't recognise, call your bank's fraud line now.
Otherwise, follow up with your bank or customer as usual.

unsure.title: Let's be safe
unsure.summary: We couldn't tell what happened. When in doubt, Mgadi always starts with the safest step.

steps.title: If money moved, call your bank's fraud line now.
steps.why: Your bank is the only one who can try to stop a payment.
do: Pick your bank below and call the official fraud line.
Write down the reference number.

steps.title: Keep the evidence.
steps.why: Whatever happened, the bank and SAPS will want it.
do: Save the emails, messages and proof of payment, and add them below.

payment.question: Did the supplier confirm that the bank change was genuine?

money.question: Has any money left your account because of this?

Microsoft 365 / Outlook: Outlook on the web: Settings (gear) > Mail > Rules. Delete rules you did not create.
Settings > Mail > Forwarding. Turn off forwarding you did not set up.
Recent sign-ins: go to mysignins.microsoft.com and look for places or devices you don't know.
Gmail / Google Workspace: Gmail: Settings (gear) > See all settings > Filters and Blocked Addresses. Delete filters you did not create.
Settings > Forwarding and POP/IMAP. Remove forwarding addresses you don't know.
Recent sign-ins: go to myaccount.google.com/security and check Your devices and Recent security activity.
Other email: Look in settings for Rules, Filters or Forwarding and remove anything you did not set up.
Ask your email or website provider to show you recent sign-ins.

whoElse.what: Open a fraud case at your nearest police station and keep the case (CAS) number. Take this incident pack.
If you have business or cyber cover, tell them today. Ask if social-engineering or funds-transfer loss is covered.
If you have an IT person or provider, ask them to check the mailbox and devices.
If the hacked mailbox held personal information about clients or staff, you may need to report a security compromise under POPIA section 22. This is not legal advice: check with a professional.
